overview.title: 📖 Overview: Barrels, Pillars, and a Pit-Side Eiruv
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 8a–8b
overview.hebrewSource: תַּשְׁמִישׁ עַל יְדֵי הַדְּחָק לָא שְׁמֵיהּ תַּשְׁמִישׁ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Daf 8 works through a series of concrete objects and spaces to sharpen exactly what makes something count as the public domain. It opens with a round reed barrel thrown into the street, testing whether its width or its loose, protruding reed-ends determine its status, then turns to Ulla's ruling that a nine-handbreadth pillar counts as public domain because people rest their burdens on it — and asks whether the same applies to a pit of equal depth. A close reading of the mishna about a shallow swamp yields the key distinction between mere passage under duress, which still counts, and use under duress, which does not — a principle then tested against a baraita that validates an eiruv placed in a pit. The daf closes by working out, through elimination, exactly what kind of threshold the Tosefta's 'exempt domain' must be.

slides.title: 🪣 A Round Barrel Thrown Into the Public Domain
slides.subtitle: Ten handbreadths tall — does its width make it an independent domain?

nodes.content: ❓ One throws a round reed barrel, ten handbreadths tall, into the public domain. Is he liable for carrying an object, or did he throw in an independent private domain that never truly 'entered' the public domain?

columns.label: Diameter under 6 handbreadths
columns.content: Abaye: LIABLE — too narrow to be its own private domain, so the law treats it as a mere object

columns.label: Diameter 6 handbreadths or more
columns.content: Abaye: EXEMPT — wide enough to count as an independent private domain in its own right

nodes.content: 🌾 Rava disagrees entirely: EXEMPT regardless of width — the loose reed-ends of the weave inevitably poke up above ten handbreadths, so no part of the barrel ever fully entered the public domain's zone

🔄 Turned mouth-down instead: Rav Ashi holds one is liable even at seven-and-a-half handbreadths — lavud (treating a 3-handbreadth gap as sealed) applies only to real partitions, not the rim of a barrel

callout.label: Underlying question:
callout.text: Every version of this case asks the same thing: has the thrown object truly come to rest within the public domain's own airspace, or has some part of it escaped that zone entirely?

slides.title: 📏 Nine Handbreadths and the Question of Pits
slides.subtitle: Ulla's graded scale of how a protrusion — or a depression — relates to the public domain
rows: Part of the public domain itself
The multitudes step directly on it — lavud treats it as touching the ground
Neither public domain nor an independent domain
Too high to be trodden on, too low for people to rest a burden there
People do rest their burdens (מְכַתְּפִין) on a protrusion that tall
A pit of the same depth (a hole, not a pillar)
Disputed: Rav Yosef says the same rule applies; Rava says it does not
Rava: using a pit is inconvenient — 'תַּשְׁמִישׁ עַל יְדֵי הַדְּחָק לָא שְׁמֵיהּ תַּשְׁמִישׁ,' use under duress is not called use

callout.label: The core dispute:
callout.text: Rav Yosef treats a hole exactly like a pillar of equal depth; Rava insists that stepping down into a pit is fundamentally less convenient than resting a load atop a raised pillar.

slides.title: 🕳️ Passage Under Duress vs. Use Under Duress
slides.subtitle: A close reading of the swamp mishna settles Rava's distinction

steps.content: 1️⃣ Mishna: where the public domain passes through a shallow swamp (רְקָק מַיִם, under ten handbreadths deep), throwing an object four cubits into it creates liability, exactly as in ordinary public domain
2️⃣ The mishna repeats this ruling for BOTH the dry season and the rainy season — necessary, since each season gives its own reason to doubt the swamp still counts
3️⃣ It also repeats 'the public passes through it' twice, which otherwise seems redundant

4️⃣ Conclusion: PASSAGE through an area, even inconvenient passage, still counts as passage and establishes public-domain status — but mere USE (standing, placing an object) under duress does NOT count as use

callout.label: Applies the distinction:
callout.text: This is exactly the line Rava draws between a nine-handbreadth pillar (use is convenient) and a pit of the same depth (use is under duress).

slides.title: 🍽️ An Eiruv Placed in a Pit
slides.subtitle: Testing 'use under duress' against a baraita that validates the eiruv

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: One who intends to establish his Shabbat residence in the public domain, and places his eiruv food in a pit less than ten handbreadths deep — his eiruv IS valid.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But that pit is only a karmelit! If use under duress isn't real use, how could placing food there ever validly establish an eiruv?

lines.speaker: Rava, first answer
lines.text: Sometimes both he and his eiruv are together in the karmelit — the baraita loosely calls his spot 'public domain' only to mean 'not a private domain.'

lines.speaker: Rava, second answer
lines.text: Or: he stands in true public domain, his eiruv in the karmelit — following Rebbi's own view that rabbinic shevut decrees were never applied during the fleeting moment of twilight, when the eiruv need be usable only an instant.

callout.label: Not a dodge:
callout.text: Rava insists these answers are not mere excuses — the swamp mishna's own redundancy independently proves the passage/use distinction is real.

slides.title: 🚪 Process of Elimination: What Kind of Threshold?
slides.subtitle: The Tosefta permits taking and giving on a threshold — but which threshold?

boxes.title: Not a Public-Domain Threshold
items: If it were public domain, taking from the homeowner would mean carrying out of the private domain — forbidden outright

boxes.title: Not a Private-Domain Threshold
items: If it were private domain, taking from the poor person would mean carrying in from the public domain — forbidden outright

boxes.title: Not Even a Karmelit Threshold
items: Even without Torah liability, a karmelit is rabbinically prohibited
The Tosefta permits this threshold ab initio — something a karmelit could never allow

callout.label: By elimination:
callout.text: The threshold must be a true exempt domain, under four by four handbreadths — where, per Rav Dimi citing Rabbi Yochanan, people from both the public and private domains may rest burdens there, as long as they never exchange objects between the two sides.

summary.principle: Public-domain status depends on genuine, convenient use — a nine-handbreadth pillar people rest burdens on counts, a pit of equal depth may not, and mere passage under duress still counts as passage even where use under duress does not count as use; the mishna's exempt-domain threshold survives only because it is smaller than four by four handbreadths.

flowSteps.content: 🪣 A round barrel's status in the public domain hinges on whether any part of it truly stays within ten handbreadths
📏 Ulla: a nine-handbreadth pillar counts as public domain since people rest burdens on it — but does a pit of equal depth?
🕳️ The swamp mishna proves: passage under duress still counts as passage; use under duress does not count as use

columns.content: 🍽️ A pit-side eiruv is still valid — reconciled through twilight's lenient rabbinic status
🚪 The mekom patur threshold survives only by being smaller than four by four

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: only genuine, convenient use — not mere physical presence or occasional passage — turns a space into public domain

quiz.q: According to Abaye, when is one liable for throwing a ten-handbreadth-tall round barrel into the public domain?
o: Only if the barrel is empty
When its diameter is under six handbreadths, since it is then too narrow to count as its own independent private domain
Only on a weekday
Never — barrels are always exempt
quiz.e: Abaye holds that a barrel narrower than six handbreadths in diameter cannot form its own private domain, so it is treated as a mere object landing in the public domain.

quiz.q: Why does Rava disagree with Abaye and rule that one is exempt regardless of the barrel's diameter?
o: Because barrels are never considered objects
Because the loose reed-ends of the barrel's weave inevitably protrude above ten handbreadths, so no part of it ever fully entered the public domain's zone
Because the public domain has no height limit
Because Rava holds that throwing is always permitted
quiz.e: Rava reasons that the protruding reed-ends always extend beyond ten handbreadths, meaning the barrel is never entirely contained within the public domain's ten-handbreadth airspace.

quiz.q: According to Ulla, at what height does a pillar standing in the public domain become part of the public domain itself?
o: Three handbreadths
Nine handbreadths, since people rest their burdens on a protrusion that tall
Twenty handbreadths
Any height at all
quiz.e: Ulla teaches that below three handbreadths people simply step on it (already ground level), between three and nine it is used by no one, and at nine handbreadths people begin resting burdens on it, making it public domain.

quiz.q: What is the difference between 'passage under duress' and 'use under duress,' as proven from the swamp mishna?
o: There is no difference between them
Passage under duress still counts as passage and establishes public-domain status; use under duress does not count as genuine use
Both are always disregarded
Both always establish public-domain status equally
quiz.e: The swamp mishna's deliberate repetition shows that even inconvenient passage counts as passage, but standing or placing an object somewhere inconvenient does not count as genuine use — this is why a pit differs from a pillar.

quiz.q: Why must the threshold described in the Tosefta, where a person may take from and give to either a homeowner or a poor person, be smaller than four by four handbreadths?
o: Because larger thresholds are always locked
Because if it were a full public, private, or even karmelit domain, this activity would be forbidden or at least rabbinically prohibited — only a true exempt domain under 4×4 permits it outright
Because the Tosefta specifies an exact measurement in cubits
Because thresholds are never halakhically significant
quiz.e: By process of elimination, the Gemara shows the threshold cannot be public domain, private domain, or even karmelit — each would make the described activity forbidden — leaving only a true exempt domain under four by four handbreadths.
